text: You finally catch the train home after a long day. All you want is your bed.
The second you sit down, the fatigue hits. A small nap couldn't hurt.
If only you knew how wrong you'd be.
You wake up to silence. Just the clack of the tracks.
Every passenger hides behind a newspaper. Nobody moves.
Two fourteen in the morning. No signal.
The route map lists stops you've never heard of.
Across the aisle, an old woman knits a scarf so long it trails across the floor.
She's the only one not reading. She's watching you.
When your eyes meet, her face falls.
"Oh no," she whispers. "Not another one."
"Where are we?" you ask.
"I'm not sure, sweetheart. I wish I knew."
She sits down beside you. "I'm June. Fell asleep too?"
You nod. "Long day." "They always are," June says.
"Where were you headed?" she asks. "Elm Street."
June glances at the map. Elm Street isn't on it.
"Okay," June says quietly. "Then listen to me carefully."
She presses a folded sheet into your hands. "Do exactly what it says."
Rule one. Do not make eye contact with the other passengers.
Rule two. When the conductor asks for your ticket, smile. Do not speak.
Rule three. If the lights go out, keep your eyes closed until the doors chime.
Rule four. Never go into the last car.
Rule five. If someone calls your name, it isn't them.
Rule six. Your stop is the one that shows your name. Get off, no matter what's on the platform.
Rule seven. Do not fall asleep again.
Rule eight. If your reflection blinks before you do, look away.
Rule nine. If the passengers start copying you, freeze.
Then, from the end of the car: click. Click.
A tall conductor comes down the aisle, punching tickets. His cap hides his eyes. Not his smile.
A man in a red tracksuit films him. "Bro, is this a prank show?"
"Ticket, please." The man starts to argue. June kicks his shoe, hard.
He blinks, then grins. Click. The conductor moves on.
Then he's at your seat. "Ticket, please."
In your pocket is a ticket you never bought. You smile. Click.
June stares at the hole, then holds up her own ticket. It's punched so many times it looks like lace.
"One hole," she whispers, "for every stop you miss."
"Watch this," the man in red laughs, and waves at the passengers.
Every newspaper drops. Every hand in the car waves back.
"Freeze," June hisses. You go still. He doesn't.
He stands and bows. They all stand and bow. He laughs. They laugh, silently.
Then every passenger takes one step toward him.
The lights go out.
When the lights flicker on, his seat is empty.
On the floor lies a newspaper. Front page: a man in a red tracksuit.
